title: What Ends Up in the Rubbish: A Household Food Waste Study

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Every year, enormous quantities of edible food are thrown away long before they reach a plate, yet most research on this problem has focused on wealthy nations. A 2024 study published in PLOS ONE set out to measure the problem somewhere less studied: Bogor Regency, an area of West Java, Indonesia, that includes both a fully urban district and a largely rural one. Over the course of a year, researchers followed 215 households, 150 in the urban sub-district of Cibinong and 65 in the rural sub-district of Sukajaya, to find out not just how much food they discarded but what kind, and why.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Rather than relying on households to estimate their own waste, which tends to produce unreliable figures, the research team physically collected, sorted and weighed the solid food waste from each home's rubbish over eight consecutive days, using digital scales accurate to two grams. Discarded drinks were tracked separately: participants kept a seven-day diary noting the type and amount of any beverage poured away. Housewives in each household were also interviewed about shopping habits, storage practices and the reasons behind particular instances of waste.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The headline figure was striking: across the whole regency, households threw away an average of 77 kilograms of food per person every year. Just over a third of this, about 29 kilograms, was still perfectly edible when discarded; the remaining 48 kilograms consisted of inedible parts such as fruit peels, bones and eggshells that are a normal by-product of cooking rather than genuine waste.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The most unexpected finding was the gap between urban and rural households. City dwellers in Cibinong generated 79.4 kilograms of food waste per person a year, almost double the 45.8 kilograms recorded in rural Sukajaya, and a significantly higher proportion of the urban total, 38.2%, was edible food compared with 23.4% in rural areas. The researchers linked this partly to income: urban households earned and spent nearly twice as much as their rural counterparts, and higher income has repeatedly been associated with looser food-purchasing habits.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Rice and other cereals accounted for the single largest share of edible waste, at nearly 17 kilograms per person annually, with vegetables close behind. Individual items told a similar story: households discarded an average of 14.2 kilograms of rice a year, alongside smaller but still notable amounts of carrots, cabbage, tofu and tempeh. Among inedible waste, fruit and vegetable peelings, dominated by banana and mango skins, made up the largest category by far.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Beverages made up a smaller but still measurable part of the total: households poured away an average of 0.3 kilograms of coffee and 0.2 kilograms of tea per person each year, most often because a pot or cup had been made larger than anyone actually wanted to finish. The researchers also noted an important boundary of their method: they measured only what ended up in household rubbish bins, which accounted for 82.8% of all discarded food in the sample. Food that was composted, fed to animals or disposed of in some other way outside the regular bin was not captured in the main waste totals, meaning the true scale of food loss, particularly in rural areas where composting was more common, may be somewhat higher than the headline figures suggest.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: When asked why food had been thrown out, householders in both districts gave strikingly similar answers. Spoilage and mould accounted for most losses of rice, vegetables, bread and packaged goods; changes in texture explained much of the waste among meat, fish, eggs, tofu and tempeh; and short shelf life was blamed for bread in particular. Cooking more rice or side dishes than a family could eat, and food left unfinished on a plate, were also common. Dairy products were frequently forgotten at the back of the refrigerator until they had to be discarded.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Despite these similar reasons, rural households ended up throwing away far less, largely because of what they did instead of putting food straight in the bin. Rural families were considerably more likely to turn scraps into compost or animal feed, keeping the material out of the waste stream altogether. Urban residents, by contrast, tended to favour convenience and were more prone to buying more than they needed, a pattern the researchers connect to busier schedules and greater purchasing power rather than carelessness.

paragraphs.label: I
paragraphs.text: The authors argue that food waste policy in Indonesia, as in many countries, has focused on collection and disposal rather than prevention, and that meaningful reductions will depend on tackling the specific items and behaviours identified in the study, rather than treating food waste as a single undifferentiated problem. They recommend urban campaigns aimed specifically at rice, vegetables and legumes, alongside wider efforts to help households extend the shelf life of perishable goods. They also note that their figures come from a single eight-day snapshot and do not capture how waste might change across seasons, so longer studies are needed before their findings can guide national policy with full confidence.
